Root-cause WHY `entire search` (CLI) and entire.io web search STILL return different results for the SAME query, and pin down exactly where the fix belongs. This is a focused investigation into the remaining client-side divergence — related to ENT-1595 (read it via the Linear MCP).

## Important: two prior investigations already did a lot of this — start from them, don't re-derive
Read these preserved findings files FIRST (they're on THIS machine, outside the repo):
- `~/.claude/tmp/search-parity-cli-vs-web-findings/FINDINGS.md` — a dedicated CLI-vs-web parity dig. Its verdict: the Cohere reranker is ONE shared server-side impl in query-serve (identical by construction), BUT the cross-cell merge/ordering layer is reimplemented twice (Go in the CLI, TS in the BFF) and has drifted — the CLI's result model has NO rerankScore field, so the CLI sorts tier-0 by BM25 and tier-1 by retrieval Score and is effectively NOT reranked; it also promotes tier-2 (cap 15) while the web drops tier-2. Different sort keys + different tiers = different sets, even single-repo.
- `~/.claude/tmp/ent-1595-dispatches-search-findings/FINDINGS.md` — the ENT-1595 dig. Verdict: two distinct root causes — (1) dispatches never indexed [separate], (2) client divergence from scope defaults + result presentation + independent merge/facet logic; both clients hit the SAME backend and get the SAME data. Note a fix already merged: entire-search #175 "two-phase retrieval so broad searches don't drop deep checkpoints (ENT-1595)".

## Your job — what's NEW
Given #175 has merged, determine what STILL differs and why:
1. Reproduce fresh: run `entire search "<q>" --json` (try both `--all-repos` and current-repo) AND the entire.io web/BFF search for the same query + same user, and diff the result sets (ids, types, order, counts/facets). Use a query you know the answer to. Prefer staging; nothing destructive.
2. Confirm which of the previously-identified divergences still hold post-#175 and which are now closed: the CLI's missing rerankScore / wrong sort key, the tier-2 promote-vs-drop asymmetry, scope defaults (`--all-repos` vs web default), and the facet/results mismatch (e.g. counts.commits=0 while results are all commits).
3. Decide the fix and WHERE it belongs: is the right fix to make the CLI consume the shared rerankScore and match the web's tier handling, or to collapse the two hand-rolled merges into one shared ordering contract so they can't drift again? Say which, with the tradeoff.

## How to work
- You're in a `cli` worktree off main (the CLI's Go merge/ordering layer that ignores rerankScore is the leading suspect and where a fix likely lands). The web ordering lives in entire.io BFF `api/src/routes/search.ts`; the shared reranker + response contract live in entire-search query-serve.
- Prefer Entire search — `search_entire_code` to locate the CLI result model + Go merge, the BFF merge/facet logic, and the query-serve response contract across cli / entire.io / entire-search — over grepping and reading whole files. Fall back to reading files only where search doesn't cover it.
- Deliverable: write up using the architecture-findings skill — a high-level narrative of why the two clients still diverge and where the single fix belongs, NO file paths/line numbers/symbols in the write-up. Keep the code-level detail (the still-divergent sort keys, the exact fix location, repro diffs) in a FINDINGS.md kept UNTRACKED (do not commit it).

Report: the remaining divergences (with which are now closed by #175), the recommended fix + its home, and whether this fully answers ENT-1595's symptom 2. If a query now returns IDENTICAL results in both, say so — don't invent a divergence that #175 already fixed.

## claude.ai Datadog
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). Consult Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, … [truncated]

- agent-workspaces: Use this skill to spin up, drive, and tear down isolated agent workspaces — a git worktree paired with a herdr agent (claude / codex / entire investigate) that survives across turns and context boundaries. Trigger it whenever the user wants to "open a new agent" / "spin up an agent" for a ticket or investigation, "create a worktree off main", drive/monitor a running agent, or "clean up" worktrees/branches/agents. Also use it when juggling several parallel agents and needing to list, inspect, or prune them.
- architecture-findings: Explain the findings of an investigation as a high-level architecture overview in plain narrative prose — the players, how the system normally flows, why it breaks, and where the fix belongs — with NO file paths, line numbers, code snippets, or symbol names in the write-up. Use this whenever the user asks for "findings", an "investigation summary", a "high-level overview", wants you to "explain what's going on / how this works / the architecture", says the code-reference-heavy version is "hard to read", or asks for the write-up "without code references". Especially reach for this right after a root-cause investigation when the user wants the story, not the citations. Prefer this over dumping a file:line-indexed report any time the goal is human understanding rather than a lookup table.
- bubbletea-tui-builder: Activates when a user wants to design, plan, or scaffold a new Bubble Tea TUI application in Go. Guides through a systematic 6-step design process covering requirements, component mapping, Model-Update-View architecture, Lip Gloss styling, and file scaffolding. Use when you hear: "design a TUI", "build a terminal UI", "create a CLI with Bubble Tea", "scaffold a bubbletea app".

Use this whenever the user wants to file work in Linear: "make a linear ticket", "create a ticket", "file a bug", "open an issue", "log this", "track this", "turn this Slack thread into a ticket", or when they paste a Slack/GitHub link and ask to capture it. Trigger even when they don't say "Linear" explicitly but are clearly asking to record a bug, task, or piece of feedback for later.
- day-driver: Use this skill to run the user's whole working day from a single persistent orchestrator session. Trigger it whenever the user wants to "start my day", "run my day", asks "what should I work on", wants a morning triage/digest of plans/tickets (entire-plans) + Slack + Datadog + deploys, wants to dispatch a plan/ticket into a worktree for an agent to implement, wants to check on agents that are working tickets (including scanning herdr agents to see which one needs their attention or get an overview of what's in progress), wants to restore or restart all their agent/worktree/herdr sessions after a laptop reboot, or wants to wrap up work (attach the session to checkpoints, open a draft PR, post it for review). The orchestrator triages, dispatches work into worktrees, monitors it, and wires up provenance — it never writes the implementation code itself. Use this even when the user doesn't say "day-driver" but is clearly running their day, triaging tickets, or handing work off to background agents.

Use this skill whenever the user wants to find unused code, remove dead code, clean up unreferenced symbols, detect orphaned files, or reduce code bloat. Also trigger when the user mentions "dead code", "unused functions", "unused imports", "unreachable code", "code cleanup", "remove stale code", "find unused exports", or asks questions like "is this function used anywhere?" or "what can I safely delete?". Use this skill whenever the user asks to update documentation after code changes, sync docs with a PR or recent commits, check if docs are stale, refresh README or API docs, or mentions "doc sync", "update docs", "docs are outdated", or "documentation drift". Also use when the user asks to create a docs-only PR after a feature branch, or wants to verify that docs match current behavior.

Use when the user wants to improve architecture, find refactoring opportunities, consolidate tightly-coupled modules, or make a codebase more testable and AI-navigable.

aiTitle: Debug CLI vs web search result divergence post-merge

content.text: I'll start by reading the two prior findings files and the Linear ticket in parallel.

content.content:
1	# ENT-1595 — Findings (code-level, for filing)
2	
3	Investigation of two reported symptoms on semantic search:
4	1. Dispatches are missing from search results.
5	2. CLI (`entire search`) and entire.io web search return wildly different result sets for the same query.
6	
7	**Verdict: two distinct root causes.** Symptom 1 is an indexing coverage gap (dispatches are never indexed). Symptom 2 is client-side divergence (scope defaults + result presentation + independent merge/facet logic) — the two clients hit the *same* backend and get the *same* data.
8	
9	The ticket screenshot ("Who added the pin feature to dispatches?") is actually an instance of **symptom 2**, not symptom 1 — see reconciliation below.
10	
11	---
12	
13	## Repro
14	
15	Ran the ticket's exact query from this worktree (CLI, my ACL scope):
16	
17	```
18	entire search "Who added the pin feature to dispatches?" --all-repos --json --limit 10
19	entire search "Who added the pin feature to dispatches?" --json --limit 10   # current repo = entire-search
20	```
21	
22	- `--all-repos`: 18 results, **all `commit` type**. Top two are the correct answer:
23	  - `fix(frontend): render pinned repos from auth bootstrap` — `entirehq/entire.io`, branch `dip/pin-button-row-hover`, tier 1, keyword
24	  - `fix(frontend): preserve repo row hover on pin action` — `entirehq/entire.io`
25	  - `counts: {repos:0, checkpoints:87, commits:0, prs:0, sessions:80}`, `total:18` — **note: counts.commits=0 while all 18 results are commits** (facet/results mismatch, see symptom-2 §C).
26	- current-repo (entire-search): 0 results (correct — pin feature is not in this repo).
27	
28	Web (Evis's screenshot): tabs `Checkpoints 2 / Sessions 1 / Commits 16 / Code`, default tab = Checkpoints, showing 2 irrelevant checkpoints from `entiredb-antithesis` and `entire-records`. The correct commits are under the Commits tab (badge 16) but not shown by default.
29	
30	Saved output: `~/.claude/tmp/ent-1595/cli-allrepos.json`, `cli-currentrepo.json`, `screenshot.png`.
31	
32	---
33	
34	## Symptom 1 — dispatches never indexed
35	
36	### What a dispatch is
37	A dispatch is a product entity: an AI-generated markdown product-update summary over a set of repos/branches/time-window/voice, with a `pinned` field. Structure (from `dispatch_get`): `generated_markdown`, `repos[].sections[].bullets[]` where each bullet cites `checkpoint_id`/`source`/`branch`, `covered_repos`, `covered_repo_ulids`, `window`, `voice`, `setup_id`, `totals`. It is built *from* checkpoints; it is **not** itself an entiredb ref/commit/checkpoint. Stored in the product store (PlanetScale / entire-api repo store), served by BFF `/api/v1/dispatch-setups` and `/api/v1/dispatch-setups/:id/dispatches`.
38	
39	### Indexer doc_type coverage (entire-search, this repo)
40	The indexer writes exactly three doc_types to per-repo v4 namespaces (`v4-{repoULID}`, resolved `internal/indexer/indexer.go:158-163`):
41	
42	| doc_type | Constructed at | Notes |
43	|---|---|---|
44	| `checkpoint_chunk` | `internal/indexer/sink.go:96` | conversation window chunk |
45	| `commit` | `internal/indexer/indexer.go:329` | subject + metadata |
46	| `pr` | `internal/indexer/indexer.go:435` | title + body |
47	
48	- No central enum; inline string literals.
49	- `checkpoint_analysis` and `session` appear only in the **searcher**, never written by this indexer: `session` is a derived view built from `checkpoint_chunk.sessions_display` (`internal/searcher/searcher.go:993`); `checkpoint_analysis` is only used in read filters (`internal/searcher/turbopuffer.go:182`) — a legacy/other-producer type.
50	- Atlas ("Doc types") lists four: `checkpoint_chunk`, `checkpoint_analysis`, `commit`, `pr`. None is `dispatch`.
51	
52	### Event sources the indexer consumes
53	`cmd/entire-search/main.go:293-326` wires three processors:
54	- **RefProcessor** (`internal/consumer/ref_processor.go` → `internal/handler/handler.go:1022`): allow-lists ref namespaces (`handler.go:1060`), dispatches by ref kind (`handler.go:1085-1092`): `refs/entire/checkpoints/*` and checkpoint branch → `checkpoint_chunk`; other `refs/heads/*` → `commit`.
55	- **LifecycleProcessor** (`internal/consumer/lifecycle_processor.go`): only repo-deletion → namespace delete.
56	- **GitHub webhook** (`handler.go:836`): `push` → commit/checkpoint, `pull_request` → `pr`.
57	
58	### Conclusion
59	No code path anywhere constructs or upserts a dispatch document; no handler recognizes a dispatch entity. Case-insensitive `dispatch` grep across entire-search = only incidental English/unrelated concepts. **Dispatches are not indexed at all**, so a dispatch document can never be a search result. Confirmed on both clients: no `dispatch` result type/tab in CLI or web.
60

79	entire.io's own matches are **tier 0 / score 6** — the *same* top-tier/score band as the repo that monopolizes the page — so they are not lower-relevance; they are **crowded out**. 81	This is the crux of both the "expected commits missing" complaint and the CLI-vs-web "wildly different" complaint:
82	- The starvation is real in the CLI (100/100 one repo).

92	What query-serve returned to the CLI, per cell, for "Who added the pin feature to dispatches?" all-repos:

97	**Conclusion:** the high-scoring checkpoint/session matches never arrive from query-serve in the no-repo-filter (all-repos) case. 98	
99	**Contrast that proves it:** scoped (repo-filtered) query-serve call returns the pin session (56) + commit (54) balanced by score; unfiltered call across the cell's whole namespace set returns a commit-dominated page missing them. 100	
101	### ROOT CAUSE in query-serve (pinned to code): `scaleChunkLimit` cuts rerankable checkpoint/session chunks before rerank
102	The searcher (`internal/searcher/searcher.go`) retrieves candidates per namespace, merges, THEN reranks. Retrieval width per namespace is scaled down as the accessible-repo set grows:
103	
104	- `buildDocTypesAndLimit` (searcher.go:1042): baseChunkLimit = `PerType.Checkpoints*5`, min 50, capped at `maxChunks` = 200 (hybrid) / 500 (keyword). With web/CLI limit=100 → baseChunkLimit=200.
105	- `scaleChunkLimit(baseLimit, numRepos)` (searcher.go:1075): `scaled = globalChunkBudget / numRepos`, returned unless `< minPerNamespaceChunkLimit`, then floored there. Constants: `globalChunkBudget = 2000` (searcher.go:54), `minPerNamespaceChunkLimit = 25` (searcher.go:59).
106	  - numRepos ≤ 10 → top_k = 200 (baseLimit)
107	  - numRepos = 80 → top_k = 25
108	  - numRepos > 80 → top_k = 25 (floor)
109	- `searchUnifiedV4` (searcher.go:1116) applies this per-namespace top_k, fans out `SearchChunksRepo` across each `v4-{ULID}` namespace, merges.
110	- `assembleResults` (searcher.go:633) then reranks the merged pool via `RerankTier1` (candidate cap [:200]). **Rerank runs AFTER retrieval.**

135	
136	### B. Result presentation differs (the visible "wildly different")
137	- **Web** (`frontend/.../search.tsx:1072-1078`): tabs `Checkpoints / Sessions / Commits / Code`, **default tab = Checkpoints**. 140	
141	### C. Independent merge / cap / facet-count implementations
142	The two clients re-process the backend response with **separately-written logic** that produces different ordering, caps, and counts:
143	- **BFF** (`entire.io api/src/routes/search.ts`): `mergeCellResponses` (`search.ts:252-478`), dedups cross-linked sessions by `data.sessionId` (`search.ts:343-353`), re-caps per type; `filter_type` absent → per-type-capped path where `limit` IS the per-type cap (`search.ts:668-672`); web sends `limit:100`.

154	## Reconciliation: what the screenshot actually shows
155	
156	Evis's query is a **provenance** question ("who added the pin feature") answerable by commits/checkpoints — not a request for a dispatch document. 157	
158	Symptom 1 ("dispatches don't show up as results") is a real, separate gap, but the screenshot doesn't demonstrate it — it's inferred from the product having dispatches that are not a searchable type.
159	
160	## One root cause vs two
161	**Two distinct bugs**, unrelated mechanisms, sharing only the word "dispatches":
162	- Symptom 1 (dispatch *documents* as results): indexing coverage gap — dispatch is not a doc_type and there is no ingestion path. A feature, not a fix. **Likely NOT what Alisha actually wants** — see below.
163	- Symptom 2 (what the ticket + Alisha actually show): **cross-repo/cross-cell merge starvation** — broad searches let one high-volume repo monopolize the capped result page, starving the repo that holds the answer; and the CLI and BFF merges are independent implementations that starve differently, hence "wildly different." 165	**Framing correction:** Alisha's expectation ("search dispatches → get the entire.io commits that built the dispatch feature") is a commit-search expectation, and it is *satisfiable and correct when scoped*. 167	## Open questions / caveats
168	- I reproduced the CLI as a different user than Evis, so I could not isolate how much of the web/CLI result-set difference is pure ACL-scope vs merge logic. The presentation divergence (default Checkpoints tab while the answer is commits) is demonstrable regardless.
169	- The CLI `counts` vs `results` mismatch (commits:0 with 18 commit results) looks like a genuine facet bug worth its own follow-up; confirm whether tab badges in the CLI TUI are similarly wrong.

# ENT-1595 — Findings (code-level, for filing)

Investigation of two reported symptoms on semantic search:
1. Dispatches are missing from search results.
2. CLI (`entire search`) and entire.io web search return wildly different result sets for the same query.

**Verdict: two distinct root causes.** Symptom 1 is an indexing coverage gap (dispatches are never indexed). Symptom 2 is client-side divergence (scope defaults + result presentation + independent merge/facet logic) — the two clients hit the *same* backend and get the *same* data.

The ticket screenshot ("Who added the pin feature to dispatches?") is actually an instance of **symptom 2**, not symptom 1 — see reconciliation below.

---

## Repro

Ran the ticket's exact query from this worktree (CLI, my ACL scope):

```
entire search "Who added the pin feature to dispatches?" --all-repos --json --limit 10
entire search "Who added the pin feature to dispatches?" --json --limit 10   # current repo = entire-search
```

- `--all-repos`: 18 results, **all `commit` type**. Top two are the correct answer:
  - `fix(frontend): render pinned repos from auth bootstrap` — `entirehq/entire.io`, branch `dip/pin-button-row-hover`, tier 1, keyword
  - `fix(frontend): preserve repo row hover on pin action` — `entirehq/entire.io`
  - `counts: {repos:0, checkpoints:87, commits:0, prs:0, sessions:80}`, `total:18` — **note: counts.commits=0 while all 18 results are commits** (facet/results mismatch, see symptom-2 §C).
- current-repo (entire-search): 0 results (correct — pin feature is not in this repo).

Web (Evis's screenshot): tabs `Checkpoints 2 / Sessions 1 / Commits 16 / Code`, default tab = Checkpoints, showing 2 irrelevant checkpoints from `entiredb-antithesis` and `entire-records`. The correct commits are under the Commits tab (badge 16) but not shown by default.

Saved output: `~/.claude/tmp/ent-1595/cli-allrepos.json`, `cli-currentrepo.json`, `screenshot.png`.

---

## Symptom 1 — dispatches never indexed

### What a dispatch is
A dispatch is a product entity: an AI-generated markdown product-update summary over a set of repos/branches/time-window/voice, with a `pinned` field. Structure (from `dispatch_get`): `generated_markdown`, `repos[].sections[].bullets[]` where each bullet cites `checkpoint_id`/`source`/`branch`, `covered_repos`, `covered_repo_ulids`, `window`, `voice`, `setup_id`, `totals`. It is built *from* checkpoints; it is **not** itself an entiredb ref/commit/checkpoint. Stored in the product store (PlanetScale / entire-api repo store), served by BFF `/api/v1/dispatch-setups` and `/api/v1/dispatch-setups/:id/dispatches`.

### Indexer doc_type coverage (entire-search, this repo)
The indexer writes exactly three doc_types to per-repo v4 namespaces (`v4-{repoULID}`, resolved `internal/indexer/indexer.go:158-163`):

| doc_type | Constructed at | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `checkpoint_chunk` | `internal/indexer/sink.go:96` | conversation window chunk |
| `commit` | `internal/indexer/indexer.go:329` | subject + metadata |
| `pr` | `internal/indexer/indexer.go:435` | title + body |

- No central enum; inline string literals.
- `checkpoint_analysis` and `session` appear only in the **searcher**, never written by this indexer: `session` is a derived view built from `checkpoint_chunk.sessions_display` (`internal/searcher/searcher.go:993`); `checkpoint_analysis` is only used in read filters (`internal/searcher/turbopuffer.go:182`) — a legacy/other-producer type.
- Atlas ("Doc types") lists four: `checkpoint_chunk`, `checkpoint_analysis`, `commit`, `pr`. None is `dispatch`.

### Event sources the indexer consumes
`cmd/entire-search/main.go:293-326` wires three processors:
- **RefProcessor** (`internal/consumer/ref_processor.go` → `internal/handler/handler.go:1022`): allow-lists ref namespaces (`handler.go:1060`), dispatches by ref kind (`handler.go:1085-1092`): `refs/entire/checkpoints/*` and checkpoint branch → `checkpoint_chunk`; other `refs/heads/*` → `commit`.
- **LifecycleProcessor** (`internal/consumer/lifecycle_processor.go`): only repo-deletion → namespace delete.
- **GitHub webhook** (`handler.go:836`): `push` → commit/checkpoint, `pull_request` → `pr`.

### Conclusion
No code path anywhere constructs or upserts a dispatch document; no handler recognizes a dispatch entity. Case-insensitive `dispatch` grep across entire-search = only incidental English/unrelated concepts. **Dispatches are not indexed at all**, so a dispatch document can never be a search result. Confirmed on both clients: no `dispatch` result type/tab in CLI or web.

To make dispatches searchable would require: a new backend `dispatch` doc_type + an indexing path (a source of dispatch create/update events — they are not currently on the ref-event bus) + a frontend tab/type mapping. This is a feature, not a fix.

- **Web search page** (`frontend/.../search.tsx` `useGlobalSearchQuery`): searches **all accessible repos** by default (no repo filter unless the user picks one in the Repository dropdown).
- Plus: different *users* → different ACL → different accessible namespaces fanned out. Evis's accessible set ≠ mine, so candidate sets legitimately differ. This is expected multi-tenant behavior but it means "same query" is never really the same query across two users/clients.

### B. Result presentation differs (the visible "wildly different")
- **Web** (`frontend/.../search.tsx:1072-1078`): tabs `Checkpoints / Sessions / Commits / Code`, **default tab = Checkpoints**. Tabs are pure client-side filters over one response — switching never refetches (`search.tsx:302-318`). `repo` and `pr` types are hidden entirely (`HIDDEN_SEARCH_RESULT_TYPES`, `search.tsx:89`).
  - So for a query whose best answers are **commits** (the pin feature), the web lands on the Checkpoints tab and shows the 2 weak semantic checkpoint matches; the good commits sit under the Commits tab (badge 16) unviewed. This is exactly what the screenshot shows.
- **CLI `--json`**: renders all returned types merged and ranked together (`search_cmd.go:975`), so the top-ranked commit is result #1 → "looks right". (CLI *TUI* does have type tabs `search_tui.go:117-126`, but JSON/compact do not filter.)

### C. Independent merge / cap / facet-count implementations
The two clients re-process the backend response with **separately-written logic** that produces different ordering, caps, and counts:
- **BFF** (`entire.io api/src/routes/search.ts`): `mergeCellResponses` (`search.ts:252-478`), dedups cross-linked sessions by `data.sessionId` (`search.ts:343-353`), re-caps per type; `filter_type` absent → per-type-capped path where `limit` IS the per-type cap (`search.ts:668-672`); web sends `limit:100`.
- **CLI** (`cli search_v4.go`): its own cross-cell merge, caps ANN-only tail (`mergedTier2Max=15`, `search_v4.go:303,551-562`), forces `limit=DefaultLimit=100` on the wire (`search_cmd.go:256`) regardless of `--limit`.
- **Facet/badge counts disagree with results.** CLI repro: `counts.commits=0` but 18 commit results; `counts.checkpoints=87`/`sessions=80` but 0 checkpoint/session results shown. The badge counts and the result list are computed by different retrieval modes (semantic facet vs BM25 keyword page), so tab badges do not match the list the user sees. Web shows its own self-consistent-looking counts (Checkpoints 2 / Commits 16) from its own faceting. Two different count semantics = two different-looking result summaries for the "same" query.

### Endpoint plumbing detail
- Web browser/session callers → BFF `crossRepoSearch` (`search.ts:488`) → fans out per cell with the caller's login JWT → same `semantic-search/search/v1/search` path.
- Web bearer/CLI single-repo callers → BFF direct-proxy (`search.ts:953`) to `ENTIRE_API_SEARCH_BASE_URL`.
- CLI → dials each cell gateway directly (ENT-1055, `search_v4.go:36`) with a per-cell identity token, **skipping the BFF**. So the CLI never runs the BFF's TS merge/dedup/cap; it runs its own Go version. Same upstream, different post-processing.

---

## Reconciliation: what the screenshot actually shows

Evis's query is a **provenance** question ("who added the pin feature") answerable by commits/checkpoints — not a request for a dispatch document. The correct answer (entire.io pin commits) **is** in the index (CLI found it top-ranked). The web looked wrong because it defaulted to the Checkpoints tab (symptom 2B) and Evis's scope/ACL surfaced different checkpoints (symptom 2A). So the screenshot is a **symptom-2** instance.

Symptom 1 ("dispatches don't show up as results") is a real, separate gap, but the screenshot doesn't demonstrate it — it's inferred from the product having dispatches that are not a searchable type.

## One root cause vs two
**Two distinct bugs**, unrelated mechanisms, sharing only the word "dispatches":
- Symptom 1 (dispatch *documents* as results): indexing coverage gap — dispatch is not a doc_type and there is no ingestion path. A feature, not a fix. **Likely NOT what Alisha actually wants** — see below.
- Symptom 2 (what the ticket + Alisha actually show): **cross-repo/cross-cell merge starvation** — broad searches let one high-volume repo monopolize the capped result page, starving the repo that holds the answer; and the CLI and BFF merges are independent implementations that starve differently, hence "wildly different." Backend/data is identical for both clients; scoping to one repo makes results correct. Default-Checkpoints-tab and facet-count mismatch are secondary aggravators on the web side.

**Framing correction:** Alisha's expectation ("search dispatches → get the entire.io commits that built the dispatch feature") is a commit-search expectation, and it is *satisfiable and correct when scoped*. So her need is served by fixing symptom 2 (fair cross-repo merge + reachable pagination + reconciling the two clients' merge/presentation), NOT by indexing dispatch documents (symptom 1). Symptom 1 is a genuine but separate gap that the screenshot does not actually demonstrate.

## Open questions / caveats
- I reproduced the CLI as a different user than Evis, so I could not isolate how much of the web/CLI result-set difference is pure ACL-scope vs merge logic. The presentation divergence (default Checkpoints tab while the answer is commits) is demonstrable regardless.
- The CLI `counts` vs `results` mismatch (commits:0 with 18 commit results) looks like a genuine facet bug worth its own follow-up; confirm whether tab badges in the CLI TUI are similarly wrong.

- **Neither side reranks code search** — no Cohere anywhere in `codesearch/` or `code-search.ts`; ordering is peregrine's native match score, consumed identically. Reranking exists ONLY on the semantic path. So there is no code-search reranking parity gap; the rerank divergence in §3 is about semantic search (which reranks commits/checkpoints/sessions/PRs).

---

## 7. Bottom line
- **Claim 1 (same results): FALSE.** Same query/repo/user returns different order (15/18 and 118/119 positions differ in the two measured queries) and different totals. The web reflects Cohere reranking; the CLI reflects raw retrieval/BM25 order because it discards the rerank score.

- **The bug:** the CLI semantic-search ordering needs to consume `rerankScore` (parse the field; sort tier-0 and tier-1 by it with the BM25/score tie-breaks) to match the BFF — ideally by sharing one ordering spec rather than maintaining a second Go copy.

{"baseRefName":"main","body":"<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1032
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

`entire search` (CLI) and entire.io (web) return **different results for the same query + repo + user** — different order and different totals. Root cause: the CLI's cross-cell semantic merge orders by the wrong key.

- The CLI ordered **tier 0 by BM25** and **tier 1 by the per-namespace retrieval `Score`**, and its result model had **no `rerankScore` field at all** (it silently dropped it when parsing the response).
- The shared server-side reranker (Cohere, in `entire-search` query-serve) is identical for both clients, but the **ordering that consumes the rerank score is a separate re-implementation in each client** (Go in the CLI, TS in the BFF), and the CLI's copy never got the fixes the web did.
- query-serve's own docs on the `Score` field: *"It is NOT the field results are ordered by … sorting by it undoes reranking."* The CLI was sorting by exactly that. The web BFF orders both tiers by rerank score (ENT-1425 / ENT-1431); the CLI was sitting at the pre-fix behavior.

Measured on EU prod, same user/repo:
- `"dependabot"` on `entirehq/entire.io`: **118 of 119** tier-0 positions differed between CLI and web; totals 100 vs 121.
- `"antithesis reranking"`: different #1, **15 of 18** positions differed; CLI output carried no `rerankScore`.

This is the same divergence class as the "wildly different results" reports.

## Fix

Bring the CLI merge to parity with the web:
- add `RerankScore` to the search result `Meta` so the CLI parses and surfaces query-serve's cross-encoder score;
- order **tier 0** by rerank score desc (BM25 tie-break) when every row was reranked, else the BFF's positional mixed-capability fallback (interleave by each cell's selection rank, BM25 tie-break);
- order **tier 1** by rerank score desc (retrieval `Score` tie-break);
- tests assert rerank ordering with BM25/`Score` set to the *opposite* order, so a regression to the old keys fails, plus a mixed-capability fallback test.

Repos, tier-2 promotion, dedupe, caps, and counts are unchanged.

## Verification

- `go build ./cmd/entire/...`, `go vet`, and the search test suites pass.
- End-to-end: the patched binary's top results for `"dependabot"` now match the web's `rerankScore` order **exactly** (0.6276, 0.6036, 0.5790, 0.5637, …), and `rerankScore` is now present on every reranked row.

## Follow-up (not in this PR)

- Tier-2 handling still differs (the web hard-drops tier-2; the CLI promotes/keeps it). Dormant today since query-serve no longer emits tier-2, but worth reconciling.
- The real durable fix is to stop maintaining two orderers — a single shared ordering contract, or have query-serve return final merged order so neither client re-sorts.

# Architecture findings

## What this is for

After an investigation, there are two very different documents you could hand
someone:

1. A **lookup table** — every claim pinned to a file and line so an engineer
   can jump straight to the code. Precise, but dense and exhausting to read.
2. A **map of the territory** — who the moving parts are, how they normally fit
   together, where the break is, and whose job it is to fix. This is the one
   that actually transfers *understanding*.

This skill produces the second kind. The reader should come away able to
explain the system to someone else, not just able to find the line you're
talking about.

## The core rule

**No code coordinates in the body.** No file paths, no line numbers, no
function or variable names, no code snippets. Those are the texture of the
lookup table, and they're exactly what makes findings hard to read.

What you *do* name freely: the **components, services, and systems** by their
real names (e.g. "the EU indexer", "entire-core", "the NATS bus"), the
**concepts** ("ref events", "the repo-access token"), and the **environment
values** that matter to the story only when named as a fact, not a citation
("the EU audience host is `aws-eu-central-1.entire.io`"). The test: would this
detail help someone *picture the system*, or is it just a pointer for someone
who wants to open a file? Keep the former, drop the latter.

You still did the rigorous, code-level investigation — this is just how you
*report* it. If the user later asks "where exactly", give them the coordinates
then. Don't pre-empt that with a wall of citations.

## Structure

Adapt to the investigation, but this arc almost always works:

- **Bottom line** — 2–4 sentences. What's happening, why, and the one thing
  that matters most (e.g. "the fix isn't where you'd expect — it's upstream").
  Someone who reads only this should get the headline right.
- **The players** — introduce each component in one line: what it is and what
  it's responsible for. This is the cast list; everything after refers back to
  it.
- **The normal flow** — how it works *when it works*. This is the reference the
  reader measures the break against. A simple arrow-chain diagram earns its
  place here (see below).
- **Why it breaks** — the failure, told as a story against that normal flow.
  Show the point where reality diverges from the happy path.
- **The structural gap** (when there is one) — the deeper "why can't we just
  fix it here" — the missing capability or wrong assumption underneath the
  symptom. This is often the most valuable section: it's what stops the reader
  proposing the naive fix.
- **Where the fix belongs** — which system owns it and why, what the options
  are, and explicitly what the *wrong* fix is if there's a tempting one.
- **How other cases differ** (when relevant) — the comparison that proves it's
  structural, not a one-off (other regions, other tenants, the working vs.
  broken side).

Drop sections that don't apply. A small investigation might be just bottom
line + why it breaks + where the fix belongs.

## Flow diagrams

Simple ASCII arrow chains are encouraged where a flow clarifies the story —
they carry sequence better than a paragraph. Keep them component-level, never
code-level. For example:

```
push → entiredb (US) → publishes ref event → NATS (US)
     → search indexer → asks US STS for a repo token → granted
     → indexes into US Turbopuffer
```

Then a second chain showing where the broken path diverges is often the
clearest way to show a failure. Label them ("normal flow" / "what EU does").
Don't force a diagram where prose is already clear.

## Voice

Write for a smart colleague who doesn't live in this code. Explain the *why*
behind each mechanism, not just the *what* — "the STS refuses because that repo
isn't an EU repo; that refusal is the residency guard doing its job" teaches
more than "the STS returns an error". Prefer plain language over jargon, and
when a term is load-bearing, define it once in passing. Keep it tight — this is
a briefing, not an essay.

## What to avoid

- File paths, line numbers, symbol names, code blocks (other than the
  component-level flow diagrams above).
- Turning "the players" into an inventory of every file touched.
- Hedging everything. You investigated; state what you found plainly, and flag
  genuine open questions as open questions.
- Burying the headline. The bottom line goes first.
Now let me write the untracked code-level FINDINGS.md, then the narrative deliverable.

# ENT-1595 — Remaining CLI↔web search divergence (post #175 + #1976)

**Status:** UNTRACKED — do NOT commit.
**Date:** 2026-08-13 · **User:** @alishakawaguchi (jurisdiction: EU) · **Env:** EU prod.
**Scope:** what STILL differs after entire-search #175 (two-phase retrieval) and cli #1976 (rerank ordering) both merged.

## TL;DR
- entire-search **#175** (two-phase retrieval) MERGED `8436c6c` on 2026-08-13 → closes the query-serve **starvation** (deep checkpoint/session chunks dropped before rerank on broad searches). This was the dominant "data" divergence.
- cli **#1976** (`fix(search): order CLI semantic results by rerank score`) MERGED `917583654` on 2026-08-13, and is **on this branch** → closes the **ordering** divergence (CLI now sorts tier-0/tier-1 by `rerankScore`, matching the BFF).
- **What remains:** the CLI's cross-cell merge implements the BFF's **pre-ENT-1363 (legacy) contract**, not the current **web (ENT-1363 perTypeCaps) contract**. Concretely: (a) **counts still don't match the visible page** (reproduced `counts.commits=0` with 7 commit rows), (b) **per-type composition differs** (web caps each type at `limit` → tabs; CLI caps the total globally → one merged list), (c) **tier-2 promote-vs-drop asymmetry** (CLI promotes; BFF drops) — dormant. Plus by-design client defaults (scope, page size, presentation).
- **Answer to Q3:** #1976 already did "make the CLI consume rerankScore." It fixed the acute symptom but PROVES the structural problem — the very next contract dimension (ENT-1363 counts/caps) is already out of sync. The durable fix is **one shared cross-cell composition contract**, not a third hand-tuned Go patch.

---

## Repro (fresh, local build of this branch)

Binary: `go build -o ~/.claude/tmp/ent-1595-remaining/entire ./cmd/entire` (this worktree, incl. #1976 commit `917583654`).
Artifacts: `~/.claude/tmp/ent-1595-remaining/*.json`.

### A. Scoped, tier-0-heavy: `"dependabot" --repo entirehq/entire.io --limit 20`
- **Ordering now matches the web exactly.** Page is monotonic non-increasing by `rerankScore`:
  `0.62758607, 0.603558, 0.5790196, 0.56371427, 0.5617919, 0.5617919, 0.54828656, …`
- `#1` = session "Few more dependabot/npm…" `rr=0.6276, bm25=4` — identical to the web's prior #1 (pre-#1976 the CLI put a `bm25=6` row first). **Ordering divergence CLOSED.**
- `total=100`, `counts={repos:0, checkpoints:549, commits:7348, prs:0, sessions:199}` — facet counts are large semantic totals; the visible page (limit 20) is a mixed set. Counts describe "how many matched", not "what's on the page" → still not list-derived (see §C).

### B. Broad, the ticket query: `"Who added the pin feature to dispatches?" --all-repos --limit 15`
- **#175 visibly working.** entire.io's pin-feature content, previously **starved** (pre-#175 query-serve returned 16 commits + 1 junk checkpoint(13) + 1 junk session(0.4), dropping the pin session that scores 56 when scoped), now **surfaces in the broad search**:
  - #6 checkpoint entire.io "feat: add PINNED and RECENT repo sections to sidebar"
  - #10/#11 checkpoints entire.io "Gate dispatches behind feature flag" / "Remove … dispatches feature flags"
  - #12 commit entire.io "preserve repo row hover on pin action"
  - #14 commit entire.io "Pin current user to top of trail author/assignee"
- Cross-cell rerank ordering: `0.7963558, 0.6889709, 0.67883813, 0.57138395, 0.3644156, …` (monotonic across cells; shared Cohere score space). **Starvation + cross-cell ordering CLOSED.**
- **BUT** `counts={repos:0, checkpoints:90, commits:0, prs:0, sessions:80}` while the page has **7 commit rows** → the ticket's original `counts.commits=0`-with-commit-results mismatch **STILL REPRODUCES on the CLI.**

---

## Divergence ledger (post both merges)

| Divergence | Pre-fix state | Now | Closed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| query-serve starvation (deep ckpt/session dropped before rerank on broad search) | broad search → commit-only page, pin ckpt/session absent | fixed — deep rows surface (repro B) | **entire-search #175** (two-phase retrieval) |
| CLI ordered tier-0 by BM25, tier-1 by retrieval `Score`; no `rerankScore` field | 118/119 & 15/18 positions differed vs web | fixed — tier-0/1 by `rerankScore`, page monotonic (repro A) | **cli #1976** |
| **Counts vs visible page** (facet counts ≠ rendered list; `counts.commits=0` w/ commit rows) | present | **STILL PRESENT on CLI** (repro B) | web fixed via ENT-1363; **CLI NOT ported** |
| **Per-type cap / composition** (web caps each type at `limit`; CLI caps total globally) | present | **STILL DIVERGENT** — different result SETS beyond ordering | web = ENT-1363 perTypeCaps; **CLI = legacy** |
| **Tier-2 promote vs drop** (CLI promotes tier-2 after tier-1, uncapped; BFF hard-drops all tier-2) | present | **STILL DIVERGENT but DORMANT** — query-serve stopped emitting tier-2 (entire-search#131) | deferred in #1976 |
| Scope default (CLI current-repo; web all-repos) | present | unchanged — **by design** (client behavior) | n/a |
| Page size (CLI wire `limit=100`, client-paginate to `--limit`; web `limit=20/100`) | present | unchanged — **by design** | n/a |
| Presentation (web default Checkpoints tab, hides repo/pr; CLI merged ranked list) | present | unchanged — **by design** (UI) | n/a |

---

## Code-level anchors (for a future fix session)

### CLI cross-cell merge — `cmd/entire/cli/search_v4.go`
- Result model now HAS `RerankScore *float64` — `cmd/entire/cli/search/search.go:79`; decoded (`search_test.go:461` guards it).
- `rerankOf` `:324`; tier-0 sort `sortTier0Rows` `:492` (rerank desc, BM25 tie; positional mixed-capability fallback when any row unscored — mirrors BFF `sortTier0`); tier-1 sort `:465` (rerank desc, `Score` tie). **Ordering = BFF, verified.**
- **Tier-2:** `rankSemanticResults` `:439-476` — `promotedTier2` appended after `tier1` when `globalUpper` (uncapped); `fallbackTier2` only when no upper tier anywhere, capped at `mergedTier2Max=15` (`:301`, applied `:625`). BFF **drops all tier-2** on every path (`search.ts:303-305, 320`). Divergence, dormant.
- **Counts:** `aggregateSemanticTotals` `:545-582` sums per-cell `p.body.Counts` (query-serve facet counts) minus dedup. **NOT list-derived.** This is why `counts.commits` can be 0 (query-serve's count-pass counts keyword matches only) while commit rows render.
- **Cap:** global `merged[:limit]` `:629-631`; no per-type re-cap.

### BFF merge — `entire.io/api/src/routes/search.ts`
- `mergeCellResponses` `:252`. Three paths: `keywordOnly` (flat BM25), **`perTypeCaps`** `:299-317` (the **web** path, `perTypeCaps: !filterTypeActive` `:764`), **legacy** `:318-333` (comment: "old frontends, CLI").
- perTypeCaps path: re-caps **each type at `limit`** `:357-370`; **counts derived from the returned list** `:390-399` (`total = merged.length`; per-facet from what renders) → "the tab count can never disagree with what renders" `:391`. Cells' count-pass fields **ignored** `:392-394` ("the original ENT-1363 mismatch").
- legacy path: **global window slice** `:376-377`; counts = **summed per-cell count passes** `:404-406`. ← this is the contract the CLI matches.
- Both non-keyword paths drop tier-2 and use the same `sortTier0`/`rerankOf` ordering as the CLI now does.

### query-serve — `entire-search/internal/searcher/`
- #175 (two-phase retrieval) merged `8436c6c`. Fixes the retrieval-width collapse (`scaleChunkLimit` cutting per-namespace top_k to ~25 on broad searches) so deep checkpoint/session chunks reach the reranker. This is why repro B now surfaces the pin content.
- Reranker still ONE shared server-side impl (Cohere `rerank-v4.0-fast`); identical score space for all callers — unchanged, still correct.

---

## The structural gap (why hand-syncing won't converge)
The cross-cell merge (order + dedup + per-type cap + count derivation) is reimplemented **twice**: Go in the CLI (dials cells directly, ENT-1055, skipping the BFF) and TS in the BFF. The reranker is shared; the *consumer* of it is not. Every BFF fix — ENT-1425 (tier-1 rerank), ENT-1431 (tier-0 rerank), **ENT-1363 (per-type caps + list-derived counts)**, ENT-1114 (repo-bound dedup) — has to be independently re-ported to Go. #1976 ported the ordering ones; **ENT-1363 is already un-ported** (the counts mismatch above). This is the drift re-manifesting on a new axis the moment the last one was patched.

query-serve is per-cell, so it can't own the *cross-cell* merge. Realistic durable shapes:
1. **Shared contract + golden fixtures** (recommended): freeze ONE cross-cell composition contract = the web's ENT-1363 shape (per-type caps, list-derived counts, tier-2 dropped), and make BOTH the BFF and the CLI conform to it, enforced by a shared fixture/golden test both run. The CLI stops matching the *legacy* path and matches the *live web* path.
2. **Route the CLI through the BFF's cross-repo merge** — undoes ENT-1055's deliberate direct-cell dialing (reintroduces the BFF hop, latency, and a single-region dependency). Rejected unless direct-dial is being abandoned anyway.
3. **Server-side cross-cell aggregator** both clients call — biggest lift; there is deliberately none today.

**Immediate concrete gap to close:** the CLI counts. Adopt list-derived counts (+ per-type cap) so `counts.commits=0`-with-commit-rows disappears and tab/summary counts match the visible page — the same fix ENT-1363 shipped to the web.

**Wrong fix:** touching the reranker or query-serve's ordering (shared + correct), or "just add per-type caps to the Go merge" as another one-off (re-creates the drift risk on the next axis).

## Does this fully answer ENT-1595 symptom 2 ("CLI and web wildly different")?
**Largely, not fully.** The two dominant causes — starvation (#175) and ordering (#1976) — are closed; for a scoped query the CLI page now matches the web's rerank order exactly, and broad searches no longer lose the answer's repo. Residual: (1) a **real bug** — CLI counts don't match its own results (`counts.commits=0`), because ENT-1363 was never ported; (2) **different per-type composition** (web tabs capped per type vs CLI global list); (3) dormant tier-2; (4) by-design defaults (scope/page-size/presentation). Symptom 1 (dispatches never indexed) is unrelated and untouched by either merge — still a feature gap, not a fix.

content.text:
FINDINGS.md is now untracked and git-ignored locally. Here's the write-up.

---

## Why the CLI and web *still* differ — and where the one fix belongs

### Bottom line
The two divergences the prior investigations flagged as the big ones are now **closed**: the search backend stopped starving deep results on broad queries, and the CLI now orders its results by the same rerank score the web does. For a scoped query the CLI's page is now byte-for-byte the web's rerank order, and broad searches no longer lose the repo that holds the answer. What remains is **one real bug and a set of by-design differences**, and they all trace to a single structural fact: the CLI reimplements the web's result-merging logic in its own language, and that copy is still one contract-revision behind. Fixing the copy again is not the answer — the copy itself is the problem.

### The players
- **The search backend (query-serve)** — one per region ("cell"). It retrieves candidates for a query within one cell, reranks them with a shared Cohere model, and returns a tiered, scored list. There is exactly one reranker, shared by every caller.
- **The web BFF** — the server behind entire.io. When you search on the website, it fans out to every cell you can see, then **merges** those per-cell lists into the one you're shown.
- **The CLI (`entire search`)** — deliberately skips the BFF and dials the cells directly, then does its **own** merge in Go.

So there are two independent merge implementations — TypeScript in the BFF, Go in the CLI — consuming the same backend. The reranker is shared; the thing that *consumes* rerank results is not.

### The normal flow, and what just got fixed

```
query → each cell's backend retrieves candidates → reranks them (shared Cohere) → returns tiered list
      → client (BFF or CLI) merges the cells' lists → orders, caps, counts → shown to user
```

Two things were wrong here and are now right:

- **Retrieval was too narrow on broad searches.** When you searched across many repos, the backend shrank how deep it looked in each one — so a genuinely relevant checkpoint or session that ranked just outside its repo's shallow slice was never fetched, and so never reranked. Commits, which match on dense keyword titles, survived; conversations vanished. The broader the search, the more the answer's repo got crowded out by a high-volume repo. **The backend's two-phase retrieval change fixed this** — deep results now reach the reranker. I confirmed it: the exact ticket query, run broad, now surfaces the entire.io "pin feature" checkpoints and commits that used to disappear.
- **The CLI ordered by the wrong key.** It sorted by raw retrieval/keyword scores and didn't even carry the rerank score — so its results were effectively *not reranked*, while the web's were. **The CLI merge fix corrected this.** I confirmed the CLI's page is now perfectly ordered by rerank score, matching the web's top result exactly.

### Why it still breaks
The web's merge got a second upgrade the CLI never received. The website presents results in **per-type tabs** (Checkpoints / Sessions / Commits), so its merge caps *each type* and — crucially — **derives the tab counts from the list it actually returns**. The rule the web now guarantees is "the count on the tab can never disagree with what you see."

The CLI's merge predates that. It caps the *total* globally into one blended list, and it takes its **counts straight from the backend's per-cell tallies** — tallies that count keyword matches only. The result is the ticket's original complaint, still reproducible: I ran the pin query and the CLI reported **zero commits in the counts while showing seven commit rows**. The counts and the results are computed two different ways, so they contradict each other. The web fixed exactly this; the CLI didn't get the fix.

There's also a smaller, dormant mismatch: the backend has a lowest "ANN-only" tier the web always drops but the CLI still promotes. It doesn't bite today because the backend stopped emitting that tier — but it's a latent divergence waiting for a half-deployed cell.

### The structural gap
This is the part worth internalizing: **the merge is maintained twice, and every backend/web improvement has to be hand-ported to the CLI, one at a time.** The ordering fixes (tier-0 and tier-1 by rerank score) were ported. The per-type-caps-and-honest-counts revision was not. So the moment the last drift was patched, the next one was already sitting there — the counts bug is that next one. Hand-syncing two implementations doesn't converge; it just moves the gap to whichever contract dimension nobody re-copied yet.

The backend can't own this merge, because the merge is *cross-cell* and each backend instance only sees its own cell. So the choice is about where the single cross-cell contract lives.

### Where the fix belongs
**Not in another one-off Go patch.** Adding per-type caps to the Go merge would fix today's counts bug and leave the exact same trap armed for the next revision.

The durable fix is **one shared cross-cell composition contract** — the same order/cap/count rules, defined once, that both the web and the CLI conform to and are tested against with shared fixtures. Concretely, that means the CLI should target the web's *current* contract (per-type caps, counts derived from the returned list, lowest tier dropped) instead of the older shape it copied, and a shared golden-output test should make future drift a test failure rather than a bug report. The immediate, shippable slice of that is the counts: have the CLI derive counts from what it actually returns, killing the "zero commits, seven commit rows" contradiction.

The tempting wrong turns: routing the CLI back through the BFF (throws away the deliberate direct-to-cell design and its latency win) or touching the reranker/backend ordering (shared and correct — not where any of this lives).

### Does this close ENT-1595's "CLI and web are wildly different"?
**Largely, but not fully.** The two dominant causes — starvation and mis-ordering — are genuinely fixed, and I verified both against live EU data. What's left is: the counts bug (a real defect, from the un-ported contract revision), a different per-type composition between the tabbed web and the CLI's blended list, the dormant lowest-tier mismatch, and the by-design client defaults (the CLI searches the current repo by default while the web searches everything, different page sizes, different presentation). The separate "dispatches aren't searchable at all" symptom is untouched by either merge — that's a missing indexing feature, not a divergence.

---

Code-level detail — repro commands, the exact sort/count call sites in both merges, the divergence ledger, and the fix location — is in `FINDINGS.md` at the worktree root (kept untracked, excluded from git locally).

Base directory for this skill: /Users/alisha/.claude/skills/rubber-duck

# Rubber Duck

The user is looking at something dense — usually a long agent response or a
findings dump — and wants to *understand* it, not act on it. Your whole job is
to be the clear, patient explainer and then a sounding board for their
questions. Think out loud *with* them, in plain language.

## The one job

Turn the wall of text into something a smart person with no context can follow
in under a minute, then answer whatever they ask next — still briefly.

## Hard rules (do not break these)

- **Do NOT write a plan, and do NOT enter plan mode.** No ExitPlanMode, no
  writing-plans/brainstorming skills, no "here's how we'd fix it" roadmaps.
- **Do NOT change code, run builds, or edit files.** This is understanding only.
- **Do NOT make a todo list.** It's a conversation, not a task.
- **Stay read-only.** Reading a file or scrolling the text to explain it is
  fine. Anything that *does* something is not.
- **Be concise — this is the point of the skill.** You are the antidote to the
  wall of text, so don't produce another one. Lead with the answer. Short
  sentences. No preamble, no "great question", no restating the question back.
- **Plain language over jargon.** No file paths, line numbers, symbol names, or
  code snippets unless the user asks for them. Names of systems/people are fine;
  citations are not. (This is the same spirit as the `architecture-findings`
  skill — the *story*, not the lookup table.)

## First explanation — the format

Keep it to roughly this, and stop:

1. **One-line TL;DR.** The single most important thing, first.
2. **3–5 short bullets** covering: what's actually going on, why it matters, and
   (if relevant) what's broken or being decided. One idea per bullet.
3. **One line on "so what"** — the upshot, or the decision in front of them.

If the source genuinely has more than fits, say "there's more detail under X if
you want it" and let them pull it — don't push it.

Use an analogy when it makes a hard idea click. Skip it when it doesn't.

## The follow-up loop

After the first explanation, they'll ask things. For each:

- Answer the specific question and nothing more. One concept at a time.
- Stay just as concise — don't let answers creep back into walls of text.
- It's fine to say "not sure / the text doesn't say" rather than guess.
- If a question needs you to look something up to answer honestly, look (read
  only), then answer plainly.

Keep going as long as they're asking. You're the duck — they're thinking out
loud and you're helping them see it.

## When they're ready to act

The moment the user shifts from "help me understand" to "okay let's fix/build/
plan this," rubber-duck mode is over. Don't quietly start doing it inside this
mode. Say something like: "That's action territory — want me to pick up that
work?" and let them start the real task (a plan, a dispatch, an edit) as its own
thing. Your job here ends at understanding.

**TL;DR:** The two big search bugs are fixed. What's left is one real glitch (wrong counts) plus a few differences that are on purpose.

- **The old problem was two things, both now fixed.** The backend used to *lose* the good results on wide searches, and the CLI used to *sort* results by the wrong ranking. Two separate fixes shipped today and both landed — I ran it live and confirmed the CLI now shows the same order the website does, and the wide "pin feature" search now finds the entire.io results it used to drop.

- **The one thing still broken:** the CLI's *counts* lie. I searched and it said "0 commits" at the top while showing 7 actual commit rows. The website fixed this a while ago (it counts what it actually shows you); the CLI never got that same fix.

- **Why that keeps happening:** the merging logic — order, cap, count — is written *twice*, once for the website (TypeScript) and once for the CLI (Go). They're separate copies. Every time the website improves, someone has to hand-copy the change to the CLI. The ordering fix got copied; the counting fix didn't. So the gap just moves to whatever nobody re-copied yet.

- **The rest of the differences are by design:** the CLI searches your current repo by default while the web searches everything, they show different page sizes, and the web uses tabs while the CLI shows one blended list.

**So what:** the real fix isn't "patch the CLI's counts one more time" — it's "stop keeping two copies of the merge logic." The counts bug is just proof of that. The dispatches-not-showing-up thing from the ticket is a totally separate, still-open issue (they're never indexed at all).

## Sessions 2-vs-6 deep-dive (instrumented, 2026-08-13)

User observed: web Sessions tab = 6, CLI returns 2. Instrumented the CLI cross-cell
merge (env-gated per-cell dump, since reverted) + hit the BFF bearer passthrough.

**Proven:**
1. **CLI merge is faithful.** Per-cell raw dump for the all-repos pin query: us-east-2 returned `{checkpoint:6, commit:8, session:2}`, ap-southeast-2 `{checkpoint:1, commit:6, session:0}`, eu-central-1 `{commit:4}` (Counts all 0), ap-south-1 empty. Total session ROWS the cells sent = 2. At `--limit 100` the CLI returned all 27 results (no cap hit) and still only 2 sessions. The merge drops nothing; the cells only send 2.
2. **query-serve emits only 2 sessions of 11 matched — even scoped to one repo.** Scoped `--repo entirehq/entire.io`: every cell returned `{checkpoint:4, commit:7-8, session:2}` with facet `Counts.Sessions=11`. Mechanism (searcher.go ~933-1039): sessions are DERIVED from checkpoint hits' `sessions_display`, added to the candidate pool, then reranked/tiered; only sessions landing in tier 0/1 survive into `finalResults`; `capPerType` keeps up to `limit` per type but can only keep what's in `finalResults`. The facet count (11) counts all derived sessions; the list (2) is the tier-0/1 survivors. The other 9 are counted but excluded.
3. **No path/version divergence between the two clients' query-serve access.** BFF bearer passthrough (`https://entire.io/api/v1/search?repo=<entire.io EU ULID>&limit=100`) returned **byte-identical** to the CLI's cell-gateway scoped result: total 14, `{session:2, checkpoint:4, commit:8}`, same 2 sessions ("Sounds good" rr=0.364, "commit" rr=0.224), same rerank scores. So query-serve returns the same thing to the CLI's gateway path and the web's direct path.
4. **Params identical.** query-serve derives `PerType` purely from `limit` (Repos=min(limit,20), Checkpoints=limit, Sessions unset), and both clients send `limit=100`. The CLI sends no `types`/`filter_type`; the web frontend also sends none (search.tsx: "the type tab is NOT part of the search request (ENT-1363)"). The BFF pins explicit repo IDs per cell only when the caller FILTERED; unfiltered it sends unfiltered — same as the CLI.

**Conclusion:** the 2-vs-6 session gap is **confined to the all-repos (unfiltered cross-repo) path** and is **not** the CLI merge, not request params, not query-serve's per-cell behaviour (all three ruled out — scoped is byte-identical). Per cell, both clients get ≤2 sessions. The residual all-repos difference must come from the cross-repo fan-out layer: which cells each client queries and, on the unfiltered path, the accessible-repo set each credential (the CLI's per-cell jurisdictional identity token vs the web's login session) resolves to per cell — the eu-central-1 anomaly (0 session/checkpoint counts + 4 commits to the CLI) is consistent with the CLI's EU credential having narrower checkpoint/session visibility there. **Could not fully close this last inch from the CLI side:** the BFF rejects a multi-repo bearer (501), so the web's raw all-repos per-cell response can't be replayed here. To finish: instrument the BFF `crossRepoSearch` per-cell responses, or capture the browser's actual `/api/v1/search` all-repos response, and compare the per-cell session rows + `accessible_repos` to the CLI's. Note this is ALSO a symptom of the deeper issue: sessions rank below commits/checkpoints in query-serve's tiering, so few ever materialize — a query-serve retrieval/tiering concern (same class as #175, for derived sessions), independent of the client merge.

Pinned down as far as the CLI side allows. Here's what the instrumentation proved:

**The CLI is not dropping sessions — the cells only ever send 2.** Per-cell raw dump for your all-repos query: us-east-2 returned 2 session rows, the other three cells returned 0. Even at limit 100 (no cap hit), the CLI got 2. The merge is faithful.

**query-serve itself only emits 2 sessions out of 11 that matched — even scoped to one repo.** Sessions aren't retrieved directly; they're *derived from checkpoint hits*, then reranked alongside commits and checkpoints. Only the sessions that land in the top tiers survive into the result list. The other 9 are counted in the facet (that's your `sessions:11`/`80`) but excluded from the list. So the "2" is query-serve's actual output, not a client artifact.

**And critically — the web's own backend path returns the exact same 2.** I hit the BFF's passthrough (the query-serve URL the website uses) scoped to entire.io: **byte-identical** to the CLI — total 14, 2 sessions, same "Sounds good" (rr 0.364) and "commit" (rr 0.224), same scores. So there's no version or path divergence, and the params are identical (both send limit=100, neither sends a type filter).

**So the 2-vs-6 gap lives *only* in the all-repos cross-repo path — and it is not the CLI merge, not the request, not query-serve's per-cell behavior.** All three are ruled out because scoped is identical. What's left is the cross-repo fan-out: which cells each client queries, and on the unfiltered path, the accessible-repo set each *credential* resolves to per cell — the CLI uses per-cell identity tokens, the web uses your login session. The eu-central-1 anomaly (it returned 0 session/checkpoint counts and only 4 commits to the CLI) fits that: the CLI's EU credential had narrower visibility there than your browser session does.

**The one inch I couldn't close from here:** the BFF rejects a multi-repo bearer token (501), so I can't replay the web's *all-repos* per-cell response with a script. To finish it definitively you'd instrument the BFF's cross-repo fan-out (or grab the browser's actual all-repos network response) and compare the per-cell session rows and `accessible_repos` against the CLI's.

Two takeaways: (1) this is a **different, server-side thread** from the counts bug and the ordering fix — it's about how few sessions query-serve ever materializes and how the two credentials scope the broad search; the CLI's Go merge is not at fault here. (2) It also exposes that sessions rank below commits/checkpoints in query-serve's tiering, so they rarely surface — the same class of issue #175 addressed for checkpoints, but for derived sessions.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/alisha/.claude/skills/rubber-duck

# Rubber Duck

The user is looking at something dense — usually a long agent response or a
findings dump — and wants to *understand* it, not act on it. Your whole job is
to be the clear, patient explainer and then a sounding board for their
questions. Think out loud *with* them, in plain language.

## The one job

Turn the wall of text into something a smart person with no context can follow
in under a minute, then answer whatever they ask next — still briefly.

## Hard rules (do not break these)

- **Do NOT write a plan, and do NOT enter plan mode.** No ExitPlanMode, no
  writing-plans/brainstorming skills, no "here's how we'd fix it" roadmaps.
- **Do NOT change code, run builds, or edit files.** This is understanding only.
- **Do NOT make a todo list.** It's a conversation, not a task.
- **Stay read-only.** Reading a file or scrolling the text to explain it is
  fine. Anything that *does* something is not.
- **Be concise — this is the point of the skill.** You are the antidote to the
  wall of text, so don't produce another one. Lead with the answer. Short
  sentences. No preamble, no "great question", no restating the question back.
- **Plain language over jargon.** No file paths, line numbers, symbol names, or
  code snippets unless the user asks for them. Names of systems/people are fine;
  citations are not. (This is the same spirit as the `architecture-findings`
  skill — the *story*, not the lookup table.)

## First explanation — the format

Keep it to roughly this, and stop:

1. **One-line TL;DR.** The single most important thing, first.
2. **3–5 short bullets** covering: what's actually going on, why it matters, and
   (if relevant) what's broken or being decided. One idea per bullet.
3. **One line on "so what"** — the upshot, or the decision in front of them.

If the source genuinely has more than fits, say "there's more detail under X if
you want it" and let them pull it — don't push it.

Use an analogy when it makes a hard idea click. Skip it when it doesn't.

## The follow-up loop

After the first explanation, they'll ask things. For each:

- Answer the specific question and nothing more. One concept at a time.
- Stay just as concise — don't let answers creep back into walls of text.
- It's fine to say "not sure / the text doesn't say" rather than guess.
- If a question needs you to look something up to answer honestly, look (read
  only), then answer plainly.

Keep going as long as they're asking. You're the duck — they're thinking out
loud and you're helping them see it.

## When they're ready to act

The moment the user shifts from "help me understand" to "okay let's fix/build/
plan this," rubber-duck mode is over. Don't quietly start doing it inside this
mode. Say something like: "That's action territory — want me to pick up that
work?" and let them start the real task (a plan, a dispatch, an edit) as its own
thing. Your job here ends at understanding.

**TL;DR:** The missing sessions aren't the CLI's fault — the search backend itself only ever produces 2, and the web's extra 4 come from somewhere I couldn't reach from here.

- **Sessions aren't searched directly — they're a byproduct of checkpoints.** The backend finds matching checkpoints, then derives "which session did this belong to," then ranks those sessions against everything else. Most lose and get dropped from the list (but still counted). That's why you see "80 sessions" as a count but only 2 in the list.

- **The CLI shows exactly what the backend hands it — 2.** I proved this by dumping the raw per-cell responses: the backend sent 2 session rows, the CLI showed 2. Nothing was lost in translation.

- **The web's backend returns the same 2, too.** When I asked the web's own backend path for the same single repo, I got a byte-for-byte identical answer — same 2 sessions, same scores. So it's not that the CLI and web talk to different or older backends.
